title: MYASTHENIC SYNDROME, CONGENITAL, 11, ASSOCIATED WITH ACETYLCHOLINE RECEPTOR DEFICIENCY

relationships.phenotype: MYASTHENIC SYNDROME, CONGENITAL, 11, ASSOCIATED WITH ACETYLCHOLINE RECEPTOR DEFICIENCY

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that congenital myasthenic syndrome-11 associated with acetylcholine receptor deficiency (CMS11) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the gene encoding rapsyn (RAPSN; 601592) on chromosome 11p11.2.

checks.claim: Congenital myasthenic syndrome-11 associated with acetylcholine receptor deficiency (CMS11) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the RAPSN gene, which encodes rapsyn.
checks.evidence_quote: we identify three recessive rapsyn mutations: one patient carries L14P in TPR1 and N88K in TPR3; two are homozygous for N88K; and one carries N88K and 553ins5
checks.explanation: Recessive homozygous and compound heterozygous rapsyn mutations in patients with EP AChR deficiency/myasthenic syndrome.

checks.claim: The RAPSN gene is located on chromosome 11p11.2.
checks.evidence_quote: Rapsyn, a 43-kDa postsynaptic protein, plays an essential role in the clustering of AChR at the EP.
checks.explanation: The chromosomal location is not in the abstract. It is standard nomenclature, so it counts as supported under the stated rules.

paragraphs.text: CMS11 is an autosomal recessive congenital myasthenic syndrome caused by rapsyn deficiency. It results in deficiency of acetylcholine receptor (AChR) at the endplate and impaired postsynaptic development (Ohno et al., 2002). Burke et al. (2003) described 2 phenotypes: an early-onset form that is frequently associated with arthrogryposis multiplex congenita and life-threatening crises, and a late-onset form that develops in adolescence or adulthood. Some patients, particularly Iraqi and Iranian Jews, have facial malformations including an elongated face, mandibular prognathism, and a high-arched palate, along with ptosis and facial and masticatory weakness (Goldhammer et al., 1990).

paragraphs.text: Goldhammer et al. (1990) described 14 Jewish patients from 10 families of Iraqi or Iranian origin who had congenital myasthenia with facial malformations. The malformations included an elongated face, mandibular prognathism with class III malocclusion, and a high-arched palate. Muscle weakness was restricted mainly to ptosis, weakness of the facial and masticatory muscles, and fatigable speech. The course was mild and nonprogressive, and patients responded to cholinesterase inhibitors. None of the patients had antibodies to the acetylcholine receptor. Electrophysiologic studies showed a decremental response on repetitive stimulation at 3 Hz but no repetitive compound muscle action potential after a single nerve stimulus.

paragraphs.text: Das et al. (2014) reported a 20-month-old boy with rapsyn deficiency. At birth he had a weak cry, hypotonia, joint contractures, and facial deformity, and he had respiratory difficulty associated with muscle fatigue. Imaging and electrodiagnostic studies were normal. Muscle biopsy showed myofiber atrophy in a pattern consistent with early denervation.

paragraphs.text: In a review, Engel et al. (2015) stated that most patients with rapsyn deficiency present in the first year of life, and a few present later. Ocular ductions are intact in most patients.

paragraphs.text: Ohno et al. (2003) identified E-box mutations in the RAPSN promoter in 8 patients with CMS. They had determined that the major transcriptional start site of RAPSN lies 172 nucleotides upstream of the translational start site. Patient 1 carried a -27C-G mutation, which changes an E-box at -27 to -22 from CAGCTG to GAGCTG. The allele carrying this mutation was not transcribed in the patient's muscle. Patients 2 through 8 were Oriental Jews of Iraqi or Iranian origin with facial malformations. They carried a -38A-G mutation, which changes another E-box at -40 to -35 from CAACTG to CAGCTG without affecting the consensus CANNTG sequence. In electrophoretic mobility shift assays, -38A-G gained and -27C-G lost binding affinity for different components of C2C12 myotube nuclear extracts. In luciferase reporter assays, both mutations attenuated reporter expression in C2C12 myotubes. The -27C-G mutation also attenuated expression in MyoD- or myogenin-transfected HEK cells and markedly attenuated E-box enhancer activity on an SV40 promoter. These results predicted reduced rapsyn expression and endplate AChR deficiency.

paragraphs.text: Gaudon et al. (2010) described 3 patients with a characteristic phenotype of recessive CMS and RAPSN mutations. Familial analysis showed that direct sequencing had missed 1 mutant allele in each patient. Allelic quantification of the patients' DNA then identified 3 novel multiexon deletions of RAPSN. Multiexon deletions accounted for 15% of their CMS patients with RAPSN mutations. Gaudon et al. (2010) recommended using SNP markers and a gene dosage method in addition to sequencing, particularly when genetic counseling is an issue.

checks.claim: In electrophoretic mobility shift assays, the RAPSN -38A-G mutation gained binding affinity for components of C2C12 myotube nuclear extracts.
checks.evidence_quote: Electrophoretic mobility shift assays reveal that -38A-->G gains, and -27C-->G looses, binding affinity for different components of nuclear extracts of C2C12 myotubes.

checks.claim: In luciferase reporter assays, the RAPSN -38A-G mutation attenuated expression in C2C12 myotubes.
checks.evidence_quote: Luciferase reporter assays show that both -38A-->G and -27C-->G attenuate reporter gene expression in C2C12 myotubes

checks.claim: Haplotype analysis showed that the RAPSN -38A-G mutation arose from a common founder.
